prompt.context: A greeting card manufacturer has experienced decreased profit. The CEO has asked you to figure out why.
prompt.question: Why has the greeting card manufacturer experienced decreased profit, and what should they do about it?

clarifying_info.q: Where are the greeting cards sold?
clarifying_info.a: Cards are stocked at grocery stores and pharmacies like CVS.

clarifying_info.q: How long do cards stay on shelves? What happens to unsold cards?
clarifying_info.a: Greeting cards are good for one season only. If a card does not sell by end of the season, it is shipped back to the manufacturer at their expense and discarded.

clarifying_info.q: How is the industry doing overall?
clarifying_info.a: The greeting card industry has experienced moderate growth over the years.
Competitors have experienced steady or slightly increased profit.

clarifying_info.q: How does the manufacturer earn revenue — are they paid when cards ship to the retailer or when cards sell to consumers?
clarifying_info.a: The manufacturer receives payment only when cards are sold to consumers. Unsold cards are shipped back at the manufacturer's expense.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs per card?
clarifying_info.a: COGS: $1.50 per card; SG&A: $0.25 per card; Shipping: $0.05 per card (incurred only if the card is unsold). Fixed costs: $200,000 per year (printing presses, plants, admin).

clarifying_info.q: How are our sales performing relative to competitors at the retail level?
clarifying_info.a: Our company's cards have continuously sold out in retailers, compared to competitors whose cards do not always sell out.

framework: Industry Analysis: assess market growth, competitor performance, and consumer trends (e.g., threat from e-cards)

Revenue drivers: understand the unique revenue model (paid only on consumer sale), factors affecting sales volume (card selection and supply on shelves), and the overstock vs. just-right-amount tradeoff

Cost drivers: identify fixed costs (printing presses, plant, admin) and variable costs (COGS, SG&A, return shipping for unsold cards), and note that return shipping is only triggered by unsold inventory

questions.prompt: What are the repercussions if a customer walks into a retailer and the card shelves are empty?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover: losing the sale entirely; poor brand awareness; losing customers to competitors; damaging relationships with retailers. This motivates overstocking.

questions.prompt: Is it better to overstock or to stock just the right amount?
questions.guidance: Overstocking benefits: customers prefer choices; a full shelf builds goodwill; empty shelves drive sales to competitors. Overstocking costs: return shipping ($0.05/unsold card) and variable production costs for unsold cards. The tradeoff is goodwill and sales volume vs. wasted variable cost.

questions.prompt: If greeting cards sell at $3.00 per card and fixed costs are $200,000 per year, how many cards must the manufacturer sell to break even?
questions.guidance: Calculate unit contribution margin using only costs incurred on sold cards (COGS + SG&A), then divide fixed costs by unit contribution.

math.setup: Unit Contribution = Selling Price - COGS - SG&A = $3.00 - $1.50 - $0.25 = $1.25. Shipping ($0.05) is excluded because it is only incurred on unsold cards. Break-even = Fixed Costs / Unit Contribution.

questions.prompt: (Bonus) The number of cards sold during the year depends on the number shipped to the retailer. Given the three shipment scenarios below, which should the manufacturer choose? Scenario A: ship 2,000, sell 1,900. Scenario B: ship 2,500, sell 2,200. Scenario C: ship 2,700, sell 2,300.
questions.guidance: Calculate profit for each scenario. Profit = (Unit Contribution × units sold) - (return shipping cost × unsold units). Unit contribution on sold cards = $1.25; cost on unsold cards = $0.05 return shipping + $1.50 COGS + $0.25 SG&A = $1.80 total variable cost incurred with no revenue. Compare profits across scenarios.

math.setup: For each scenario: Profit = ($1.25 × units_sold) - ($1.80 × units_unsold). Units_unsold = units_shipped - units_sold.
math.answer: Scenario B (ship 2,500, sell 2,200) yields the highest profit at $2,210.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors affect the sales volume of greeting cards at the retail level?

categories.name: Card selection
ideas: Breadth of occasions covered (birthdays, holidays, sympathy, etc.)
Design quality and differentiation vs. competitors

categories.name: Card supply on shelves
ideas: Ensuring shelves are stocked and not empty
Overstocking to give customers choices and avoid empty-shelf perception
Managing return volume to limit reverse-logistics costs

categories.name: Retailer relationships
ideas: Placement and shelf positioning within the store

categories.name: Consumer trends
ideas: Threat from e-cards reducing physical card demand

recommendation: The greeting card manufacturer should improve revenues by ensuring a wide selection and sufficient supply of cards at each retailer, while carefully managing the number of unsold cards at season end.

The increase in goodwill and brand awareness from well-stocked shelves outweighs the added variable costs of unsold cards, as demonstrated by Scenario B being more profitable than conservative stocking (Scenario A).
risks: Supplying extra cards may not be profitable if card quality lags competitors', because additional supply will not translate to additional sales.
If return shipping or production costs rise, the breakeven on overstocking shifts unfavorably.
next_steps: Conduct consumer research to understand how customers choose greeting cards (design, occasion, brand) to improve sell-through rates.
Determine if unsold cards can be repurposed or have any salvage value to reduce the cost of overstock.
Analyze SKU-level sell-through data by retailer to optimize shipment quantities at a more granular level.
